seo.best_title: How Did Ancient Women Handle Their Periods?
seo.description_hook: Ancient women had far fewer periods than we do today. Here's what they actually used, what the medical texts say, and why the monthly problem wasn't so monthly.
paragraphs: In this video we look at how ancient women managed menstruation with cloth, linen, moss and whatever was available, and why they experienced only about 100 periods in a lifetime compared to 400 today.
We cover the Kahun Gynaecological Papyrus, Deir el-Medina work records, Greek and Roman practices, menstrual huts, and the practical knowledge passed from mother to daughter.
Clear, easy explanations with the real evidence and the popular myths.
sources: Strassmann - The Biology of Menstruation in Homo sapiens, Current Anthropology (1997)

shorts.title: Ancient Women Had Way Fewer Periods
shorts.description: Modern women get about 400. Ancient women got around 100. Here's why.

shorts.title: Where 'On the Rag' Comes From
shorts.description: The most common ancient method was simple folded cloth.
shorts.pinned: Makes sense when you think about it.

shots.say: Right now, millions of women around the world are on their period.
They use a pad, a tampon, a cup, and they move on.
For most of human history, none of that existed.
No pharmacies. No disposable products. No modern underwear.
So how did ancient women actually handle their periods?
And here's the weird part. They had far fewer of them than women today.
A modern woman can have around 400 periods in her life. An ancient woman? Around 100.
That's the real story. The bodies were the same. The lifestyle was not.

shots.say: Ancient women started their periods later. Often around 15 or 16.

shots.title: BECAUSE
shots.say: Nutrition and hard living delayed the first period.
Then they spent a huge part of their lives pregnant or breastfeeding.

shots.title: WHY PERIODS STOPPED
shots.say: Breastfeeding can pause periods for months or even years.
No birth control. High child mortality. So they had many children, one after another.
Scientists studied the Dogon people in Mali. Their women averaged about 100 periods in a lifetime.
Modern women get three or four times that number.

shots.say: When the period did come, they still had to deal with it.
But almost nothing was written down about the practical side.

shots.title: WHY NO EVIDENCE
shots.say: It was private. Often taboo. And the materials they used simply rotted away.
We piece it together from medical texts, rare notes, and what traditional societies still do.

shots.say: The most common solution, almost everywhere, was simple.
Folded rags. Linen strips. Soft fabric pinned or tied in place.
Then washed and reused. That's where the old phrase 'on the rag' comes from.
In Egypt, linen was everywhere. Women used strips of linen as pads.
shots.ai: an Egyptian woman washing linen strips by the Nile

shots.say: Some stories say they used softened papyrus as early tampons. Possible, but hard to prove.
Linen and cloth were almost certainly more common.
In Greece and Rome, the same idea: homemade pads of wool or rags.
Old claims about Hippocrates describing wooden tampons are mostly mistranslations.
Those descriptions were for treating wounds or medical problems, not everyday periods.

shots.label: EGYPT
shots.say: Egypt gives us the best written evidence.
The Kahun Gynaecological Papyrus is the oldest known medical text about women's health.
It talks about the womb, fertility, pregnancy, and contraception.
shots.label: KAHUN PAPYRUS

shots.say: One method involved crocodile dung. Another used honey and natron.
It doesn't give a clear period guide, but it shows people were thinking carefully about the female body.

shots.label: DEIR EL-MEDINA
shots.say: At the workers' village of Deir el-Medina, scribes kept attendance records.
Women sometimes took days off for 'hesmen' — their word for menstruation.
That's rare. Most places never wrote it down so casually.
There are also hints of special spaces, and the red tyet amulet linked to protection.

shots.say: In other places, women used whatever grew nearby.

shots.title: LOCAL MATERIALS
shots.say: Moss, soft grass, plant fibers. In some areas, even animal hide or sea sponges.
Some women simply free-bled into their clothing, especially if the flow was light.
In some cultures, menstruating women stayed in special huts outside the village.
shots.label: MENSTRUAL HUT

shots.say: The Dogon still do this in traditional practice. It makes the timing public.

shots.say: Greek and Roman writers had strong ideas about the body.
They thought a woman's body was softer and held more fluid. Periods released the extra blood.
The Roman writer Pliny claimed menstrual blood could sour wine, kill bees, and rust metal.
Wild exaggerations. But they show how powerful and mysterious the process seemed.
In Egypt, menstrual blood sometimes appeared in remedies, linked to the power of creating life.

shots.say: Most of the real knowledge never got written down.
Mothers told daughters. Sisters told sisters.
Women shared what worked with the cloth they had, the plants nearby, and the rules of their community.
They managed with less frequency, simpler materials, and a lot of practical skill.

shots.title: THE DIFFERENCE
shots.say: From cloth and river water, to modern products and more frequent cycles.
Today we have better products and more choice. But we also have far more periods in a lifetime.
The bodies are the same. The lifestyle changed.
So next time you reach for a pad or a cup, remember how it used to be done.
Folded cloth, practical knowledge, and women who just got on with it.
